                    ### Question
                    During an experiment conducted to alter the infectivity of common viruses that affect humans, an investigator successfully increases the host range of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The new strain of the virus can infect fibroblast-like cells in addition to the usual target of HIV. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the increase in the host range of the virus?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Mutation of the gene coding for viral surface glycoproteins
opb. Point mutations in the hemagglutinin gene
opc. Increased rate of budding out of host cells
opd. Reassortment of genetic material between segments of two viruses
ope. Excessive activity of viral RNA polymerase

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The most likely explanation for the increase in the host range of the virus is the mutation of the gene coding for viral surface glycoproteins. This mutation alters viral attachment and entry mechanisms, allowing infection of new cell types, which results in an increased host range of the virus. Point mutations in the hemagglutinin gene could also contribute to changes in viral receptor specificity and enable infection of fibroblast-like cells, expanding the host range. Evidence paths related to cells interacting with genes and host factors support the concept of genetic changes influencing host range expansion.
